traveler: Saint Acacius of Byzantium (Agathius, Achatius, Ahac, Sant'Agazio, San Acato)
title: The Centurion Under Two Names: Perinthus, Ararat, and the Company of Fourteen
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Caesarea Mazaca, the province that gives him no town
stops.date_confidence: placeholder: the sources say only 'born in the late 3rd century in Cappadocia' and name no town, no parents and no year. The year 280 has no source support and stands here to force a pin; the coordinate is Caesarea Mazaca, the province's chief city, used as a regional proxy and not as a claimed birthplace
stops.campa: Cappadocia gives the empire horses, wool and soldiers, and in the last quarter of the third century it gives it a boy whose name will come down in half a dozen spellings. The sources name the province and nothing smaller: no town, no parents, no year. Caesarea Mazaca stands here as the province's chief city and as an admission, since the natal ground of Acacius is not recorded anywhere the tradition can reach. He is a Greek of Cappadocia, and he takes a commission in the legions of a state that has not yet decided what to do about Christians.
suggested_refs: The Cappadocian recruitment grounds of the eastern legions in the third century

stops.name: Nicomedia, the edict that reaches the rank
stops.date_confidence: attested for the edict: Lactantius dates the demolition of the church to 23 February 303 and the posting of the first edict to the following morning. The link to Acacius's arrest specifically is reconstruction; no source names him in connection with the edict
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of February the prefect's men level the church that stands in sight of Diocletian's palace, and the next morning the first edict goes up: churches razed, scriptures surrendered, Christians stripped of rank and of standing at law. Constantine is thirty and at court that week, and says nothing anyone recorded. The edict does not name Acacius. It names his rank, since a soldier holding rank is exactly what the order strips, and every account of the centurion's arrest begins from the machinery started here.
sources: constantino_el_grande.journey.json, stop 'Nicomedia, the church pulled down'
suggested_refs: The Diocletianic edict of 24 February 303, first of four against the Christians

stops.name: Perinthus, the tribune Firmus asks the question
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the Passio names Perinthus and the tribune Firmus but gives no month; March 303 is placed here only to keep the arrest between the February edict and the May feast
stops.campa: The tribune Firmus, holding Perinthus on the Propontis, puts to his centurion the question the edict requires him to put. Acacius answers that he is a Christian and is arrested on that answer alone. Perinthus is a port town of Thrace, later called Heraclea, a short sail from a garrison town that has no great name yet; the road out of it runs east along the water. Nothing in the Passio suggests the tribune wanted this. The law had reached the rank, and the rank had to be asked.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Acacius of Byzantium', citing the Passio
suggested_refs: Perinthus-Heraclea in Thrace, modern Marmara Ereglisi, seat of the Thracian command

stops.name: The Thracian road, the voice heard on the march
stops.date_confidence: unlocated: no milestone or place is named for this episode. The coordinate is the midpoint of the coastal road between Perinthus and Byzantium, chosen because the format requires a pin, and it should be read as a guess rather than a fix
stops.campa: He is marched east under guard with other prisoners, the water on his right the whole way. The Synaxarion says a voice out of the air speaks to him on this road, and that the men chained beside him hear it too and are converted by it. No milestone marks the place. The pin sits at the road's midpoint between the town where he was taken and the city where he will be killed, which is a guess dressed as a coordinate, and the tradition offers nothing finer than the sentence itself.
stops.quote_source: Life of 'Martyr Acacius the Centurion at Byzantium,' Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, commemorated 7 May, rendering the Greek Synaxarion
sources: Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, 'Martyr Acacius the Centurion at Byzantium' (oca.org), fetched and confirmed verbatim
suggested_refs: The eastern coastal road of Thrace between Heraclea and Byzantium

stops.name: Byzantium, seven days in the cells
stops.date_confidence: hagiographic: the seven days, the healing and the exchange with Vivianus come from the Synaxarion life and from no Roman-era document. The coordinate is the one the quotes carry, inside the old peninsula, and no prison has been excavated
stops.campa: Seven days in the cells of Byzantium and the wounds close. The officer Vivianus, finding a scourged man standing whole, assumes a bribed physician and demands the name. The Synaxarion preserves the answer, which credits no physician. This is the second of the two sentences the tradition puts in his mouth, and both come from the same Greek life, translated into English for the Orthodox Church in America's calendar of the seventh of May. No document of the persecution itself carries either one.
stops.quote: My power and strength are given me by the Lord Jesus Christ, Who has healed my wounds.
stops.quote_source: Life of 'Martyr Acacius the Centurion at Byzantium,' Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, commemorated 7 May
sources: Orthodox Church in America, Lives of the Saints, 'Martyr Acacius the Centurion at Byzantium' (oca.org), fetched and confirmed verbatim
suggested_refs: The Greek Synaxarion life of Acacius the Centurion, source of both surviving sayings

stops.name: Byzantium, scourged and beheaded
stops.date_confidence: conventional: the year is given as 303 or as c. 304 and the day follows the older feast of 8 May, which the Roman calendar later moved to 7 May and the Orthodox keep on 17 April instead. Three dates for one execution, none of them documented
stops.campa: He refuses to sacrifice, is scourged again, and is beheaded at Byzantium, a town of no particular importance holding a garrison and a customs house. The conventional year is 303, sometimes 304. The feast lands on the eighth of May in the older reckoning and the seventh in the Roman calendar, and the Orthodox keep him on the seventeenth of April. A second feast, the sixteenth of January, marks the moving of the bones. The churches that hold these dates have never sat down to compare them.
suggested_refs: The feast of 7 May in the Roman calendar and 17 April in the Orthodox, for the same execution

stops.name: Byzantium, the walnut tree nobody can find
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the site is unlocated: Socrates of Constantinople writes only that a walnut tree stood there 'on which the martyr was supposed to have been hanged.' The tree and the chapel have never been found and the coordinate is an admitted round number inside the old peninsula
stops.campa: A separate strand, reported by Socrates of Constantinople, says he was hanged from a walnut tree, and that a chapel later stood at the spot to mark it. Hanged and beheaded are not the same death. Socrates writes that the martyr was supposed to have been hanged there, which is a historian's hedge and not a record. The tree has never been located and neither has the chapel. The coordinate here is a round number placed inside the old peninsula because the story insists on a place and supplies none.
sources: Socrates Scholasticus, via en.wikipedia, 'Church of St. Acacius'
suggested_refs: Socrates of Constantinople on the walnut-tree chapel, the only witness to the hanging account

segments.name: The City Built Over the Grave

stops.name: Byzantium, the furrow traced with a spear
stops.date_confidence: attested for the foundation rites of November 324; the walking legend is preserved by Philostorgius and later chroniclers, not by a contemporary. The relation to Acacius is geographic only, and no source connects the two
stops.campa: Twenty-one years after the execution Constantine walks the line of the new walls with a spear point dragging in the dirt, out past anything Byzantium has ever enclosed, and the town where a centurion was killed for refusing to sacrifice becomes the capital of an empire that will soon require the sacrifice of no one. The two men do not meet. Constantine was at Nicomedia the week the edict went up. He is here in November of 324, and the ground he is measuring holds the grave.
sources: constantino_el_grande.journey.json, stop 'Byzantium, the furrow traced with a spear'
suggested_refs: The line of the Constantinian land wall, superseded within a century by the walls of Theodosius II

stops.name: Constantinople, a church nobody records founding
stops.date_confidence: attested that the church existed and is among the earliest of the city after the 328 foundation; the exact year is unrecorded and 330 stands for the foundation period. The dedication is hedged by the source itself as possible, not certain
stops.campa: Among the first churches raised after the foundation there is one of Saint Acacius, and nobody writes down who built it or when. The reference works place it in the fourth century and hedge the dedication as possible rather than certain: the scholar David Woods argues the patron is a different Acacius entirely, a comes under Constantine and no martyr at all. The company of fourteen will take the centurion anyway, eleven hundred years later, and will not be asked to show which Acacius it means.
suggested_refs: David Woods on the dedicatee of the Constantinopolitan church of Saint Acacius

stops.name: Constantinople, the roof comes down on Arcadius
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode in Socrates; undated within the reign. Arcadius is augustus from 383 to 408, and 400 is a midpoint placeholder, not a source date. An earlier pass gave his reign as 395-408, which is only his sole rule in the east
stops.campa: The emperor Arcadius, augustus since 383, comes to the chapel of the walnut tree, and the building falls in on itself while he is inside it. The crowd waiting outdoors is unhurt. Socrates tells it as a deliverance rather than a warning, which is how the fifth century reads architecture. The church is rebuilt. The walnut chapel is not found again. The same caveat sits over the whole episode that sits over the dedication, since the Acacius honored here may not be the Acacius killed here.
sources: Socrates Scholasticus, via en.wikipedia, 'Church of St. Acacius'
suggested_refs: Socrates Scholasticus on the collapse of the church of Saint Acacius before Arcadius

stops.name: Constantinople, the martyrium at the Heptaskalon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and outside the research pool: no atlas file and no source gathered for this journey states a martyrium of Acacius at the Heptaskalon or its restoration under Justinian. It is carried from general Constantinopolitan church topography on the atlas's canonical city pin, and should not be treated as attested
stops.campa: A martyrium of Saint Acacius is said to have stood at the Heptaskalon on the Golden Horn and to have been restored under Justinian. No atlas file states it and no source gathered for this journey states it either. It is carried here as reconstruction, on the city pin the atlas already uses for the year Barbara's relics reach Constantinople from Heliopolis. Justinian pays for the masonry in both stories, two centuries apart, and the atlas puts both martyrs on the one coordinate.
sources: saint_barbara.journey.json, stop 'Constantinople, the relics translated from Heliopolis'
reconstruction from Constantinopolitan church topography, outside the research pool
suggested_refs: The Heptaskalon quarter on the Golden Horn and its Justinianic church building

segments.name: The Other Acacius, on the Mountain

stops.name: Antioch, Hadrian gives Armenia back
stops.date_confidence: attested for the policy: Hadrian abandons Trajan's conquests beyond the Euphrates in the first months of 117 and pulls the frontier back. The connection to Acacius is geographic proximity only; the atlas file on Hadrian mentions neither Acacius nor Ararat
stops.campa: Hadrian at Antioch gives back what Trajan took. Mesopotamia and Armenia are abandoned in the first months of the reign, the frontier pulled to the Euphrates, and the highland the Romans have just stopped garrisoning is the highland where a legend will later put ten thousand crucified soldiers. The atlas already carries Hadrian through this decision. It does not carry Acacius, and no source joins the two. The geography is all that touches here, and geography is not evidence.
sources: adriano.journey.json, stop on the abandonment of Mesopotamia and Armenia, 117
suggested_refs: Hadrian's withdrawal to the Euphrates and the ungarrisoned Armenian highland

stops.name: Temple Mount, the emperor the legend names
stops.date_confidence: attested for Hadrian's decision at Jerusalem in 130; entirely reconstruction as regards Acacius. This stop marks nothing Acacius did. It marks the one emperor the Ararat dossier names, standing on ground the atlas has already fixed
stops.campa: In 130 Hadrian stands on the platform in Jerusalem and decides to build Aelia Capitolina over it, a decision that will cost Judaea a war and its name. The atlas pins him here. The Ararat dossier names him as the emperor who ordered ten thousand soldiers crucified, so the same reign carries both stories and only one of them is documented. This stop marks nothing Acacius did. It marks the emperor the legend borrows, standing on ground the atlas fixed for other reasons.
suggested_refs: Hadrian's foundation of Aelia Capitolina and the Bar Kokhba war that followed it

stops.name: The slopes of Ararat, the cross over the field
stops.date_confidence: legend, explicitly undocumented: German Wikipedia states that the story ist als historische Begebenheit nicht belegt, is not documented as a historical occurrence. The date follows the Hadrianic attribution and is the legend's date, not a historian's
stops.campa: Nine thousand Roman soldiers under a commander named Achatius are sent into Armenia to put down a revolt and are trapped by a force many times their size. The German tradition says a cross appears over the field, the whole body converts on the spot, and then wins. A barbarian contingent sent afterward to punish them converts too, and the count reaches ten thousand. German Wikipedia states flatly that none of this is documented as an event. The atlas has never carried the story at all until now.
suggested_refs: The legend of the nine thousand and the battlefield conversion in Armenia

stops.name: Greater Ararat, ten thousand crosses on the flank
stops.date_confidence: legend: the day follows the Roman Martyrology's feast of 22 June, which is a calendar date and not an event date. The summit coordinates are confirmed for the mountain and nothing else; no site of any martyrdom has ever been identified there
stops.campa: The converted legion is marched up the mountain, crowned with thorns and crucified on the slope, ten thousand crosses on the flank of the peak where the ark is supposed to have grounded. The Roman Martyrology keeps them on the twenty-second of June. The centurion of Byzantium is kept on the seventh of May. The same name leads both processions, one to a headsman in a garrison town and one to a mountain in Armenia, and the calendar prints both without comment.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Mount Ararat' for the summit coordinates only
suggested_refs: The Roman Martyrology entry for the Ten Thousand Martyrs of Mount Ararat, 22 June

stops.name: Antioch, the Greek variant under Decius
stops.date_confidence: attested as a calendar variant, not as an event: the Greek Synaxarion lists the Holy Ten Thousand Martyrs on 1 June, at Antioch, under Decius. The year 250 is the conventional Decian persecution date and stands as a placeholder
stops.campa: A Greek Orthodox variant puts the ten thousand not on Ararat but at Antioch, not under Hadrian but under Decius, and keeps them on the first of June. Three emperors, three cities, three dates, one number. The Synaxarion does not explain the move and the Roman books do not acknowledge it. Antioch is where Hadrian was standing when he gave Armenia back, which is a coincidence of pins rather than a link, and nobody who had to choose between the accounts has ever set them side by side.
suggested_refs: The Greek Synaxarion entry for the Holy Ten Thousand Martyrs at Antioch, 1 June

stops.name: Nicomedia, the myriads of the eighteenth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested as a distinct calendar entry, Myriads of Holy Martyrs, by the sword, at Nicomedia, kept on 18 March. Its relation to the Ararat and Byzantium dossiers is confusion in later calendars, not any documented link, and the year 303 is the persecution's year rather than the entry's
stops.campa: A third entry, the Myriads of Holy Martyrs put to the sword at Nicomedia, sits under the eighteenth of March, in the city and the year of Diocletian's edict. It is a separate dossier and later calendars keep confusing it with the other two. Nicomedia already holds the edict that took the centurion's rank, and holds Pantaleon the physician of the same company of fourteen, and holds the palace where Constantine learned how a tetrarchy comes apart. Three martyr traditions, one address.
suggested_refs: The 18 March commemoration of the Myriads of Nicomedia, a third unharmonized dossier

stops.name: Rome, Anastasius Bibliothecarius writes it down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the attribution: the written Ararat account is credited to Anastasius Bibliothecarius in the ninth century. The year 870 is the middle of his working life and stands as a placeholder; no source dates the composition exactly
stops.campa: The Ararat account is written down in the ninth century, attributed to Anastasius Bibliothecarius, librarian of the Roman church, some seven hundred years after the events it reports. The tradition running through the Catholic Encyclopedia calls it a legend with many historical inaccuracies and utterly improbable details, and the phrase survives into the modern reference works unchanged. This is the earliest text the dossier has. No acta survive from within a century of either Acacius.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Ten Thousand Martyrs', citing Anastasius Bibliothecarius
suggested_refs: Anastasius Bibliothecarius and the ninth-century Latin translation of eastern hagiography

stops.name: Squillace, the spring below the Vivarium
stops.date_confidence: contested, and the contradiction is the point: English and Spanish sources date the translation to about 630, near the spring of Cassiodorus's Vivarium. The Italian entry on the same saint dates it to the eleventh century. Both are carried, on the same pin, as two stops
stops.campa: Relics called Acacius's arrive in Calabria and are set by a spring near the ruins of Cassiodorus's Vivarium, the monastery of copyists on the Ionian shore. Squillace takes him as patron under the name Sant'Agazio and keeps his feast on the seventh of May. The English and Spanish accounts date the translation to about 630. The Italian account dates it four hundred years later. Neither cites the other, and the gap between them has never been argued out by anybody.
suggested_refs: The site of Cassiodorus's Vivarium near Squillace on the Ionian coast of Calabria

stops.name: Squillace, the eleventh century says otherwise
stops.date_confidence: the competing date, carried as its own stop rather than resolved: it.wikipedia, 'Acacio di Bisanzio', places the translation in the XI secolo. The year 1050 is the middle of that century and is a placeholder. The claim that the relics rest in the cathedral is unsupported by the article on Squillace itself
stops.campa: The Italian entry on the Byzantine Acacius puts the translation in the eleventh century and says the relics remain in the cathedral, though the entry on Squillace itself names the Concattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta and mentions no relics at all. Two dates for one arrival, four centuries apart, and a resting place asserted by one source and unmentioned by the other. This is a second pin on the same town because the contradiction is the fact, and picking a winner would mean inventing evidence.
suggested_refs: The Concattedrale di Santa Maria Assunta at Squillace, named without any relic inventory

stops.name: Cuenca, the Castilian name
stops.date_confidence: unattested: the Spanish source states the veneration at Cuenca under the name San Acato and gives no church, no century and no account of the transfer. The year 1400 is a bare placeholder and the coordinate is the city centre
stops.campa: A relic reaches Cuenca and the city venerates him as San Acato. The Spanish source states the veneration and nothing else: not the church, not the century, not who carried the bones over the sea from Calabria or from Byzantium. The coordinate is the cathedral city's centre, chosen because a pin is required and no building is named. The entry establishes one thing and no more: the Greek centurion already has a Castilian name by the time anyone in Spain bothers to write about him.
suggested_refs: The cult of San Acato in Castile, church and date unrecorded

stops.name: Avila, the same name and the same silence
stops.date_confidence: unattested, exactly as at Cuenca: veneration under the name San Acato is stated and nothing else is. The year is a placeholder and the coordinate is the city centre
stops.campa: Avila keeps a relic of the same saint under the same Castilian name, San Acato, and keeps the same silence: no church, no date, no account of the journey. Two walled Castilian towns three hundred kilometres apart hold pieces of a Cappadocian killed in Thrace, and the record of how they got them does not exist in anything reachable. The pin is the city centre and nothing more, and the transfer goes unrecorded at both ends of it, in Calabria and in Castile alike.
suggested_refs: The parallel Castilian cults of San Acato at Cuenca and Avila, both undocumented as to origin

stops.name: Guardavalle, the arm carried up the coast
stops.date_confidence: attested for the patronage and the 7 May feast; the year 1584 and the name of Bishop Marcello Sirleto come from the Spanish entry alone and are not independently confirmed. Wikipedia's article on Guardavalle carries the cult without the date
stops.campa: In 1584 an arm is carried up the coast to Guardavalle and Bishop Marcello Sirleto installs it there, and the town takes Sant'Agazio for patron with the feast on the seventh of May. Guardavalle is thirty kilometres from Squillace. The saint Calabria received once, whether in the seventh century or the eleventh, is now divided between two towns keeping the same day. The article on Guardavalle confirms the patronage and the feast and says nothing whatever about 1584.
suggested_refs: The arm reliquary of Sant'Agazio at Guardavalle, Calabria

stops.name: Regensburg, the fourteen gathered against the plague
stops.date_confidence: inferred
stops.campa: In the dioceses of Regensburg, Bamberg and Wurzburg, with the Black Death working through Franconia, the faithful begin invoking a fixed company of fourteen saints as a single wall. Acacius is in it from the start, assigned the headache and the fear of dying with no warning. Barbara, Catherine, Margaret, Giles, Christopher and Vitus stand in the same rank, and the atlas already carries all six. The company is a fourteenth-century German invention, a thousand years after the man it is naming.
sources: saint_barbara.journey.json, stop 'Regensburg, the Fourteen Holy Helpers gathered against the plague'
suggested_refs: The earliest Regensburg-area prayers and monastery images of the Fourteen Holy Helpers as a fixed group

stops.name: Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: inferred: by about 1400 the sequence appears closed and in a fixed order across the Franconian dioceses. No single document fixes the closing and the year is the atlas's working convention, shared with catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json
stops.campa: By about 1400 the sequence closes: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Regional lists still swap Leonard or Sebastian in and out, but the shape has hardened, and Acacius always comes first because the alphabet puts him there. The list has one bishop's name sitting in a soldier's slot, and nobody in Franconia is checking which Acacius the Greek books meant.
sources: catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, stop 'Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen'
suggested_refs: The closed Franconian sequence of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, c. 1400

stops.name: Kloster Langheim, the abbey that owns the field
stops.date_confidence: attested for the abbey and its ownership of the ground; the September date is the month before the first vision and is a positioning placeholder. The coordinates are the abbey's own, four kilometres east of the shrine, and are deliberately kept distinct from it
stops.campa: The Cistercians of Langheim own the field on the far hill and lease it out for grazing. The abbey sits four kilometres east of the place where the shepherd will see what he sees, and the two are distinct places, though later accounts and later map coordinates keep collapsing them into one point. Langheim will judge the visions, build the chapel, run the pilgrimage for three centuries and commission Neumann. The fourteen enter Franconian ground here as a landholding question.
sources: catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, stop 'Kloster Langheim, the abbey that owns the field'
suggested_refs: Kloster Langheim at Klosterlangheim, Lichtenfels, distinct from the shrine four kilometres west

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd hears a child
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of the first vision, 24 September 1445, reported by the shepherd Hermann Leicht. An earlier pass wrongly extended this year to the third apparition as well
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of September the shepherd Hermann Leicht, working the abbey's field, sees a crying child sitting in the grass. He stoops to lift it and it is gone. He tells nobody who matters. The vision returns weeks later with two candles burning beside it. Acacius is not named yet and will not be named by the child at all. He is counted into the fourteen afterward, by people working from the Franconian list, which is how most of the fourteen got there.
suggested_refs: The meadow above Langheim where Hermann Leicht saw the child, 24 September 1445

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, fourteen children in red and white
stops.date_confidence: attested: German Wikipedia dates the final apparition to 28 June 1446. The gathering pass gave 1445, which belongs to the first vision alone; the two years are routinely run together in English summaries
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of June the child comes a third time with a red cross on its breast and thirteen others around it, and speaks. The German sources date this final apparition to 1446, not to 1445, which belongs to the first sighting alone. Acacius stands in that ring by inheritance from the Regensburg list, one of fourteen faces the shepherd does not identify and the abbey identifies for him. The child gave Hermann Leicht a number. The names came later, off a list drawn up in Franconia a century before he ever saw the field.
stops.quote: We are the fourteen helpers, and wish to erect a chapel here, where we can rest. If you will be our servant, we will be yours.
stops.quote_source: The apparition to Hermann Leicht, June 1446, as preserved in the Langheim abbey tradition
sources: saint_barbara.journey.json, stop 'Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd's vision, the fourteen children'
suggested_refs: The Langheim abbey record of the third apparition, 28 June 1446

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the maidservant rises
stops.date_confidence: attested as eighteen days after the third apparition; the exact day follows from the 28 June date and the abbey's own count
stops.campa: Eighteen days after the third apparition a maid at Langheim, given up for dying, invokes the fourteen helpers and recovers. That is what moves the abbey. Not the shepherd, who is a shepherd, but a cure with witnesses to it. The pilgrimage opens, the chapel goes up, and the field takes the name Vierzehnheiligen, the Fourteen Saints. Acacius, whose assigned competence is the headache, is now the property of Franconian pilgrims who will never hear the name Perinthus spoken.
suggested_refs: The cure of the Langheim maidservant, the miracle that opened the pilgrimage

stops.name: Bern Munster, forty panels of glass
stops.date_confidence: attested for the window, made 1448-1450; the year of the losses is not given in the source. The composition is recorded as 40 rectangular narrative panels, 8 medallions and 3 decorative elements, of which 11 rectangles and 1 medallion survive
stops.campa: Two years after the Langheim cure, glaziers at the Bern Munster set the Ten Thousand Martyrs into a window: forty rectangular narrative panels, eight medallions, three ornaments. Eleven rectangles and one medallion survive. Bern fought at Laupen in 1339 and will fight at Murten in 1476, both on or near the twenty-second of June, and the city reads the coincidence as patronage. The Ararat legend has found a civic use, which legends manage faster than they find evidence.
suggested_refs: The Ten Thousand Martyrs window of the Bern Munster, 1448-1450, mostly lost

segments.name: The Painters of the Ten Thousand

stops.name: Nuremberg, the woodcut and the drill
stops.date_confidence: catalogued c. 1496-1498, usually c. 1497, described in the sources as approximately ten years before the 1508 panel. The gathering pass gave a flat 1496, which overstates the precision available
stops.campa: Durer cuts the Ten Thousand Martyrs into a block in his Nuremberg workshop, about ten years before he paints the subject. In the woodcut a bishop named Acacius stands among the tortured with his eyes stripped through by a drill. The leader of the ten thousand is a soldier in every telling of the legend. The same reference work that puts a mitre on him here gives him a centurion's rank in its other article, so the woodcut is copying a confusion it did not invent.
suggested_refs: Durer's woodcut Martyrdom of the Ten Thousand, c. 1497, with the blinded bishop Acacius

stops.name: Wittenberg, Durer paints himself into the massacre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the commission and the year of the panel; the pin is Wittenberg, the collection it was made for, rather than Nuremberg where it was painted
stops.campa: Frederick the Wise commissions the panel for his relic collection, and Durer paints himself into the middle of the massacre, in black, holding a staff with his name and the date on it, beside his dead friend the humanist Conrad Celtis. The bishop Acacius is in this version too, no longer blinded but bound in chains. Ten thousand crucifixions arranged as a landscape, with the painter standing at the centre of it looking out, is the image the legend is remembered by.
suggested_refs: Durer's 1508 panel, with the self-portrait and Conrad Celtis at the centre of the composition

stops.name: Wittenberg, the relic hoard in the Schlosskirche
stops.date_confidence: attested that Frederick the Wise's collection at All Saints' held relics of the Ten Thousand Martyrs; the year is a placeholder for the collection's early-sixteenth-century state, not a documented inventory date
stops.campa: The Schlosskirche at Wittenberg holds Frederick's collection, thousands of fragments accumulated for the indulgences attached to viewing them, and among them are relics of the Ten Thousand Martyrs. Nine years after the Durer panel arrives, Martin Luther nails ninety-five theses about indulgences to the door of the church that houses it. The relic economy that gave the Ararat legend a market in Saxony is taken apart by a man working in the same building.
suggested_refs: The relic collection of Frederick the Wise at All Saints' Church, Wittenberg

stops.name: Venice, Carpaccio takes the commission
stops.date_confidence: attested for the commission by San Giorgio Maggiore in 1515; the present location of the painting could not be established. The Gallerie dell'Accademia collection pages returned no record and no other holding institution was found
stops.campa: San Giorgio Maggiore commissions Vittore Carpaccio to paint the same subject for Venice, a second great Renaissance canvas of ten thousand crosses on a mountain nobody in the workshop has seen. Where the painting is now could not be established in this pass: the Accademia collection pages return no record of it, and no other holding institution was found. The commission is documented for the year 1515, and the canvas itself is documented nowhere after it.

stops.name: Palermo, Santi Diecimila Martiri
stops.date_confidence: the dedication is attested, the date is not: German Wikipedia names the Palermo church and the Kirche zu den Zehntausend Rittern at Lenthe without dating either. The year 1600 is a bare placeholder and the Lenthe church was not geolocated in this pass
stops.campa: Palermo keeps a church of the Santi Diecimila Martiri, and Lenthe in Lower Saxony keeps a Kirche zu den Zehntausend Rittern, the Church of the Ten Thousand Knights, which promotes the crucified legion to cavalry. German Wikipedia names both and dates neither, and the Lenthe church was not located on any map in this pass. The pin is Palermo and the century is a placeholder. Two churches carry the number in their dedication, one in Sicily and one in Lower Saxony, and that much is on record.

stops.name: Vienna, the panel relabelled
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1508 panel now hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum; no source in this pool dates the transfer out of Wittenberg or into the imperial collection. The pin takes the museum's opening year and says so
stops.campa: The panel leaves Wittenberg's devotional apparatus and ends in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, hung as a Durer rather than as an object of veneration. No source in this pool dates the transfer, so the pin takes the museum's opening year and admits it. The picture Frederick the Wise bought to certify a relic hoard is now evidence about a painter. The martyrs stay on their crosses, and the label hung under them says Nuremberg instead of Ararat.

stops.name: Idrija, quicksilver in the bucket-maker's spring
stops.date_confidence: attested with an open spread: the town's own record gives the first sighting of liquid mercury as 1490, 1492 or 1497, and attaches no saint's day to it. The coordinates are exact for Idrija
stops.campa: A bucket-maker soaking his tubs in a spring below Idrija lifts them out heavy and finds quicksilver in the bottom. The year is given as 1490, or 1492, or 1497, depending on which account is read, and the town's own record attaches no saint to it. Carniola has kept Acacius under the name Ahac since at least the sixteenth century. The story of the mountain and the mercury is about to be joined to his feast day, though not yet, and not by way of this first find.
suggested_refs: The spring at Idrija where liquid mercury was first found, dated variously 1490, 1492 and 1497

stops.name: Idrija, the lode opens on his feast day
stops.date_confidence: attested to sl.wikipedia, 'Ahac', which states that on the saint's feast day in 1508 a productive mercury vein opened at Idrija. The gathering pass credited this to es.wikipedia, 'Acacio de Bizancio', which contains no Idrija and no mercury whatever; attribution corrected
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint Ahac in 1508 a rich cinnabar lode opens at Idrija, and the town dates its mine from that day. The Slovene entry on Ahac carries the claim; the Spanish entry on Acacio de Bizancio, sometimes cited for it, contains no mercury and no Idrija at all. The first sighting in the spring and the opening of the lode are two events eighteen years apart, not a contradiction, though they are often reported as one. Idrija will work mercury for four and a half centuries.

stops.name: Sisak, the Ottoman army broken on the twenty-second of June
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle and the date; the feast-day linkage comes from sl.wikipedia, 'Ahac', not from the battle article. Command was joint, and the gathering pass named Auersperg alone. The coordinates are the Sava-Kupa confluence, the battle site, rather than Sisak town two kilometres away
stops.campa: At the confluence of the Kupa and the Sava a Habsburg force breaks an Ottoman army on the twenty-second of June, the feast of Ahac. Ruprecht von Eggenberg, Ban Tamas Erdody and Andreas von Auersperg share the command, though Carniolan memory keeps only Auersperg, whom it calls the Carniolan Achilles. The battle date and the feast date are the same date, and that is the whole of the connection. Carniola takes it for proof and builds a church accordingly.

stops.name: Gora above Mali Locnik, the church for the victory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the dedication and the reason, not for the year: sl.wikipedia states the church was built to commemorate the 1593 victory and gives no founding date. The coordinates follow sl.wikipedia, 'Mali Locnik', 45.89083/14.61291, correcting an earlier estimate that fell ten kilometres south
stops.campa: On the peak of Gora, seven hundred and forty-eight metres above Mali Locnik near Turjak, a church of Saint Ahac goes up to commemorate the victory at Sisak. The Cappadocian centurion, taken at Perinthus by a Roman tribune for refusing to sacrifice, is now a Slovene bulwark against the Ottomans, invoked by farmers who could not place Thrace on a map. The founding year is not fixed anywhere in the sources. The church is there, and the reason for it is not disputed.

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the altar that cannot be moved
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cornerstone of Balthasar Neumann's basilica in 1743; the day within April follows the atlas's existing pin in catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json
stops.campa: Balthasar Neumann sets the cornerstone of a basilica for the fourteen on the shepherd's field, and then has to build it around an error: the site foreman has laid the foundations so that the altar of grace falls in the nave instead of the crossing. Neumann does not move the altar. He redesigns the church around it, three interlocking ovals with the shrine standing free in the middle of the floor. Acacius will get his niche on that altar because the altar could not be shifted.

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, Agathius or Acacius, against headache
stops.date_confidence: attested for the consecration of 1772 and for the Mercy Altar inscription, which gives the double name Agathius or Acacius with the feast of 8 May and the patronage against headache. The modern grouping gives 7 May instead; both are carried
stops.campa: The basilica is consecrated in September 1772, thirty years after the cornerstone and nineteen after Neumann's death. On the Mercy Altar the fourteen stand in their assigned niches, and one of them is labelled Agathius, with Acacius in brackets, feast the eighth of May, invoked against headache. The standard modern list gives the seventh instead. The double name is carved into the furniture: Franconia declined to decide which martyr it honours and built a basilica on the undecided ground.
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Fourteen Holy Helpers', citing Richard Stracke, Christian Iconography, 20 October 2015

stops.name: Obernburg am Main, the ranked rows
stops.date_confidence: inferred
stops.campa: Fifty kilometres up the Main from Frankfurt, in the chapel of Saint Anne at Obernburg, Peter Vambach of Erlenbach carves the fourteen in four ranked rows with Christ at the centre. Beside the altar a plaque keeps the old rhyme naming Margaret with the worm, Barbara with the tower, Catherine with the wheel. Acacius has no rhyme and no attribute anyone can read at a glance. He stands in the rows on the strength of the list alone, which is how he has stood since Regensburg.
stops.quote: Margaretha mit dem Wurm, Barbara mit dem Turm, Katharina mit dem Radl, das sind die drei heiligen Madl.
stops.quote_source: Plaque verse, Annakapelle, Obernburg am Main

stops.name: Rome, two feasts and no ruling
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1969 reform, which removed several of the fourteen from the General Roman Calendar and decanonized none of them. That the calendar keeps 22 June and 7 May apart without adjudicating between the two Acaciuses is a reading of the calendar, not a statement any document makes
stops.campa: The calendar reform of 1969 takes several of the fourteen off the general Roman calendar. None is decanonized and the company survives in local use. The Roman books still keep the ten thousand of Ararat on the twenty-second of June and the centurion of Byzantium on the seventh of May, and no instrument anywhere states whether the two names belong to one man. The church has kept both feasts for sixteen centuries without ever being made to choose, and this file leaves the choice where it found it.
